labelled_points = gpd.read_file("labelled_points.gpkg")

training_segments, mixed_segments = label_segments(
    segments_gdf,
    labelled_points,
)

training_segments contains a feature_class column. mixed_segments contains segment IDs that intersected more than one class.

Review mixed segments before training. They often indicate label noise, poor segmentation, or sample points near class boundaries.

docs.title: Train and Predict
docs.text:
from obia.classification.classify import classify

result = classify(
    segments_gdf,
    training_segments,
    method="rf",
    n_estimators=300,
    random_state=42,
)

classified = result.classified

The classified GeoDataFrame includes:

  • predicted_class
  • prediction_margin
  • original segment geometry
  • original feature columns

docs.title: Random Forest
docs.text:
Random forest is the default starting point:

result = classify(
    segments_gdf,
    training_segments,
    method="rf",
    n_estimators=300,
    max_depth=None,
    random_state=42,
)

Use it before trying neural-network classification. It is usually easier to diagnose on small tabular feature sets.

docs.title: MLP
docs.text:
Use method="mlp" for scikit-learn's multi-layer perceptron classifier:

result = classify(
    segments_gdf,
    training_segments,
    method="mlp",
    hidden_layer_sizes=(100, 50),
    max_iter=500,
    random_state=42,
)

MLP classification is more sensitive to feature scaling, class balance, and training size.

docs.title: Reports and Explanations
docs.text:
Set compute_reports=True to calculate a confusion matrix and classification report on the train/test split:

result = classify(
    segments_gdf,
    training_segments,
    method="rf",
    compute_reports=True,
    n_estimators=300,
)

print(result.confusion_matrix)
print(result.report)

SHAP explanations require the optional explain dependency group:

pip install "obia[explain]"

Then run:

result = classify(
    segments_gdf,
    training_segments,
    method="rf",
    compute_shap=True,
    n_estimators=300,
)

docs.title: Save Output
docs.text:
classified.to_file("classified_segments.gpkg", driver="GPKG")

The output remains a vector object map. If a raster classification map is required, rasterize the classified polygons onto the source raster grid as a separate post-processing step.

docs.title: Experimental Detection
docs.text:
obia.detection is experimental. Its interfaces and workflow may change in future releases.

The package provides a RetinaNet-based object detection path for raster imagery. It is separate from the segmentation/classification workflow.

Use detection when the target output is bounding boxes. Use segmentation when the target output is image objects and object-level feature tables.

docs.title: Install Experimental Detection Dependencies
docs.text:
Install the detection extra:

pip install "obia[detection]"

The detection extra includes PyTorch, Torchvision, Albumentations, and Matplotlib.

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
TreeDetectionDataset reads raster chips and JSON annotations:

from obia.detection.dataset import TreeDetectionDataset
from obia.detection.utils import get_transforms

dataset = TreeDetectionDataset(
    image_dir="/path/to/chips",
    annotations_file="/path/to/annotations.json",
    transforms=get_transforms(train=True),
)

Annotations should provide bounding boxes and labels for each image.

docs.title: Build A Model
docs.text:
from obia.detection.models import build_detection_model

model = build_detection_model(
    num_classes=2,
    in_channels=3,
)

Set in_channels to match the number of raster bands used for detection.

docs.title: Train
docs.text:
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from obia.detection.train import train_model
from obia.detection.utils import collate_fn

loader = DataLoader(
    dataset,
    batch_size=2,
    shuffle=True,
    collate_fn=collate_fn,
)

model = train_model(
    model,
    loader,
    num_epochs=20,
    device="cuda",
)

Use device="mps" on Apple Silicon when the local PyTorch installation supports it.

docs.title: Predict
docs.text:
from obia.detection.predict import predict

detections = predict(
    model,
    image_path="/path/to/image.tif",
    device="cuda",
    score_threshold=0.5,
)

The result is a dictionary with boxes, scores, and labels arrays.

docs.title: Current Limits
docs.text: Detection expects prepared chips and annotations. It is best treated as a model-building workflow for bounding boxes, while segmentation is the starting point for object maps and object-level classification.

docs.title: Large Rasters
docs.text:
The standard segment() workflow loads and processes an image in memory. For large rasters, use tiled processing so each tile can be segmented separately.

The tiled path is currently focused on SLIC segmentation and requires GDAL Python bindings.

docs.title: Tiled SLIC Segmentation
docs.text:
from obia.utils.tiling import create_tiled_segments

create_tiled_segments(
    input_raster="/path/to/large_image.tif",
    output_dir="output_tiles",
    method="slic",
    tile_size=512,
    buffer=64,
    n_segments=1000,
    compactness=10,
)

The function writes intermediate tile outputs and a merged segment file under output_dir.

docs.title: Masked Processing
docs.text:
Pass a binary mask raster to avoid segmenting invalid or out-of-scope areas:

create_tiled_segments(
    input_raster="/path/to/large_image.tif",
    input_mask="/path/to/mask.tif",
    output_dir="output_tiles",
    method="slic",
    tile_size=512,
    buffer=64,
    n_segments=1000,
    compactness=10,
)

The mask should align with the source raster grid.

docs.title: Choosing Tile Size
docs.text:
Start with tiles that are large enough to preserve the objects you care about but small enough to keep memory use stable.

Practical starting points:

Raster size Starting tile size medium scenes 512 large scenes 512 or 1024 memory-constrained runs 256

Increase buffer when visible tile-edge artifacts appear. Larger buffers reduce boundary artifacts but increase processing cost.

docs.title: When To Use This Path
docs.text:
Use tiled segmentation when:

  • the standard segmentation path exhausts memory
  • a full-scene label image would be too large
  • you need to process many scenes with the same settings

Use standard segment() when possible. It is simpler to inspect, debug, and reproduce.

docs.title: Point Clouds
docs.text:
Point-cloud features are added to existing segment objects. Raster features and point-cloud features live on the same rows, which keeps labelling, review, and classification focused on one object table.

The recommended order is:

  1. create segment objects from a raster
  2. add point-cloud features to those segment objects
  3. label training segments
  4. classify the enriched segment table

docs.title: Install Point-Cloud Dependencies
docs.text:
Point-cloud workflows need PDAL. Install PDAL in a conda environment first, then install OBIA with pip inside that environment:

conda create -n obia-pointcloud -c conda-forge python=3.11 pdal python-pdal
conda activate obia-pointcloud
pip install obia

If you already have an environment, install PDAL from conda-forge before installing OBIA:

conda install -c conda-forge pdal python-pdal
pip install obia

The conda-forge PDAL package is usually more reliable than installing PDAL through pip because the Python bindings need the PDAL base library.

To include the optional pyforestscan reader, install the point-cloud extra after activating the same environment:

pip install "obia[pointcloud]"

docs.title: Add Features to Segments
docs.text:
import geopandas as gpd

from obia.pointcloud import add_pointcloud_features

segments = gpd.read_file("segments.gpkg")

segments = add_pointcloud_features(
    segments,
    pointcloud="/path/to/points.laz",
    metrics=["height", "intensity", "density"],
)

segments.to_file("segments_with_pointcloud_features.gpkg", driver="GPKG")

The output preserves segment rows and appends pc_* feature columns. Segment geometries are used to select points; no new object boundaries are created.

If the point cloud has no CRS, pass one explicitly:

segments = add_pointcloud_features(
    segments,
    pointcloud="/path/to/points.laz",
    crs=segments.crs,
)

docs.title: In-Memory Point Clouds
docs.text:
Point clouds can also be passed as a DataFrame:

import pandas as pd

points = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "x": [0.25, 0.75, 1.25],
        "y": [0.25, 0.75, 0.25],
        "z": [2.0, 4.0, 10.0],
        "intensity": [5.0, 7.0, 9.0],
    }
)

segments = add_pointcloud_features(
    segments,
    points,
    crs=segments.crs,
)

GeoDataFrames and NumPy arrays are also supported.

Structured arrays can use X, Y, Z, and Intensity fields. Plain NumPy arrays are interpreted as columns in this order:

x, y, z, intensity

docs.title: Feature Columns
docs.text:
Height metrics use the pc_z_* prefix:

  • pc_z_min
  • pc_z_max
  • pc_z_mean
  • pc_z_median
  • pc_z_std
  • pc_z_p5, pc_z_p25, pc_z_p50, pc_z_p75, pc_z_p95

Intensity metrics use the pc_intensity_* prefix. Density features include:

  • pc_point_count
  • pc_density

docs.title: Use in Classification
docs.text:
After enrichment, label the enriched segment table:

from obia.utils.utils import label_segments

training_segments, mixed_segments = label_segments(
    segments,
    labelled_points,
)

After labelling, train the classifier with the enriched segment table:

from obia.classification.classify import classify

result = classify(
    segments,
    training_segments,
    method="rf",
    n_estimators=300,
)

The predicted output keeps the original segment geometry and the added point-cloud columns.

docs.title: Segmentation
docs.text: This page covers the standard OBIA segmentation path: read a raster, create image objects, calculate object features, and write the resulting GeoDataFrame.

docs.title: Load a Raster
docs.text:
from obia.handlers.geotif import open_geotiff

image = open_geotiff("/path/to/image.tif")

open_geotiff() reads all bands by default. To read only selected GeoTIFF bands, pass one-based Rasterio band numbers:

image = open_geotiff("/path/to/image.tif", bands=[1, 2, 3, 4])

Once loaded, OBIA uses zero-based band indexes for segmentation_bands and statistics_bands.

docs.title: Run SLIC Segmentation
docs.text:
from obia.segmentation.segment import segment

segments = segment(
    image,
    segmentation_bands=[0, 1, 2],
    statistics_bands=[0, 1, 2, 3],
    method="slic",
    n_segments=3000,
    compactness=10,
)

The returned object stores:

  • segments._segments: the raw label image
  • segments.segments: a GeoDataFrame of segment polygons and features
  • segments.method: the segmentation method
  • segments.params: segmentation parameters passed to the algorithm

docs.title: Run Quickshift Segmentation
docs.text:
segments = segment(
    image,
    segmentation_bands=[0, 1, 2],
    method="quickshift",
    kernel_size=3,
    max_dist=6,
    ratio=0.5,
)

Use SLIC as the default starting point. Quickshift can be useful for texture-rich imagery, but it is generally more sensitive to parameters.

docs.title: Choose Bands
docs.text:
segmentation_bands controls which bands define object boundaries. Use bands with strong spatial structure and class-relevant contrast.

statistics_bands controls which bands are summarized after the segments are created. These can include bands that were not used for segmentation.

For example, segment on RGB but calculate features from RGB plus a height or vegetation index band:

segments = segment(
    image,
    segmentation_bands=[0, 1, 2],
    statistics_bands=[0, 1, 2, 3],
    method="slic",
    n_segments=3000,
    compactness=10,
)

docs.title: Save Segment Objects
docs.text:
segments.segments.to_file("segments.gpkg", driver="GPKG")

GeoPackage is a practical default because it preserves geometry, CRS, and tabular feature columns in one file.

docs.title: Add Other Feature Sources
docs.text:
The segment GeoDataFrame is the common feature table. After segmentation, additional feature sources can be joined to the same rows. For point clouds:

from obia.pointcloud import add_pointcloud_features

segments_gdf = add_pointcloud_features(
    segments.segments,
    pointcloud="/path/to/points.laz",
    metrics=["height", "intensity", "density"],
)

Use the enriched segments_gdf for labelling and classification.

docs.title: Inspect Results
docs.text:
A segmentation run should be judged spatially before classification. Check whether object boundaries are meaningful for the classes you want to predict. If a segment regularly crosses class boundaries, tune segmentation before training a classifier.

The most important SLIC parameters are usually:

  • n_segments: approximate target number of segments
  • compactness: balance between color similarity and spatial regularity
  • mask: optional mask to exclude pixels from segmentation

Increase n_segments for smaller objects. Increase compactness for more regular shapes.
